'''André Bouchard''' (January 26, 1946 &ndash; 4 March 2010) was a Canadian [[ecologist]] and [[environmentalist]] who spent most of his career at [[Université de Montréal]] (UdeM) and the [[Montreal Botanical Garden]]. His specialties included [[landscape ecology]] and plant [[community ecology]], and he received several awards during his lifetime.

==Biography==
Bouchard was born in 1946 in Montreal and grew up in [[Côte-des-Neiges]], although his family came from [[Saint-Anicet, Quebec|Saint-Anicet]], and maintained a secondary residence there.<ref name="fine"/><ref name="francoeur"/><ref name="soleil"/> His father,  Louis G. Bouchard, was a successful leather goods supplier.<ref name="fine"/> He studied first at [[Collège Jean-de-Brébeuf|Collège Jean-De-Brébeuf]] before graduating with a degree in biological sciences from Université de Montréal. He went to [[McGill University|McGill]] and [[Cornell University]] for his postgraduate studies, which he completed in the 1970s.<ref group="note">His dissertation is dated from 1975, the same year he
became curator at the Botanical Garden.</ref><ref name="forumobit"/>

In 1975 he began teaching at his ''alma mater'' Université de Montréal, while simultaneously becoming curator at the Botanical Garden.<ref name="P0173"/> He would remain at the University until his death, and at the garden for 21 years.<ref name=forumobit/> As curator, his primary duty was directing research at the garden.<ref name="gingras"/> His own research discussed the flora of [[Newfoundland (island)|Newfoundland]] ([[Gros Morne National Park]] was the topic of his doctorate dissertation) and of southwestern Quebec.<ref name="projects"/><ref name="sauve"/><ref name=thibaudeau/> His creative use of notarized acts to study the evolution of Quebec forest since [[New France]] led to significant discoveries regarding the evolution of [[beech-maple forest]]s.<ref name=sauve/>

Beyond scientific work, he rapidly became known for his involvement in various environmental issues, notably the fight to save the [[Bois de Saraguay]], an [[old-growth forest]] on the northern side of [[Montreal Island]] that was threatened by developers.{{#tag:ref|He would say of this that it was "like a fast-track doctorate in political science."<ref name=levesque/>|group=note}}<ref name=gingras/><ref name="levesque"/> Over the years, he invested himself in numerous other debates, such as those over the [[Boisé du Tremblay]] in [[Longueuil]],<ref name="boise-du-tremblay"/> the Muir Forest in [[Hichinbrooke, Quebec|Hichinbrooke]]<ref name="muir"/> (now the [[Boisé-des-Muir Ecological Reserve]]) and, closer to home, the Little and Large Tea Field, two peat bogs in his native town of Saint-Anicet.<ref name="teafield2009"/><ref name="teafield2006"/> He was also a member of the 2004 [[Commission Coulombe]] whose report was to define provincial forest exploitation policy.<ref name="coulombe"/> Although he was well aware that he and his fellow commissioner would catch flak from the industry for the recommendations (which included a 20% reductions of wood cuts), he pushed forward with the belief that these were the right decisions to make.<ref name=sauve/>

Having been a close collaborator of [[Pierre Bourque (politician)|Pierre Bourque]], he was named director of the Botanical Garden in 1994 when Bourque had to leave the position following his election as mayor.<ref name=forumobit/><ref name=levesque/> It was a short stay, both because he had notified the administration he considered it an interim position, and because he was not comfortable with the complicated administrative apparatus connected to the position.<ref name=gingras/> In 2002, he became the first director of the newly founded Institut de Recherche en Biology Végétale (IRBV), a position he occupied until 2006. All these years he continued to teach at the Université, and directed over 45 master's and doctorate students.<ref name=forumobit/> He also sat on the Montreal Heritage Council from 2006 to 2008,{{#tag:ref|About this stay, a fellow member of the Council noted: "he taught us that a council which fails to annoy is a useless council."<ref name="Tetreault"/>|group=note}} on the [[Centre hospitalier universitaire Sainte-Justine]] board of directors,<ref name=francoeur/><ref name=forumobit/> and received awards from the Quebec Association of Biologists (prix Georges-Préfontaine, 2005) and the [[Association francophone pour le savoir|Acfas]] (prix Michel-Jurdant for environmentalism, 1990).<ref name=francoeur/><ref name="thibaudeau"/>

In addition to his environmental and scientific work, he had a keen interest in history, both local and scientific. In 1998 he published a short historical account of the botanical garden, and in 2007 a compendium of correspondence from [[Marie-Victorin]]. At the time of his death, he was working on books about southern Quebec [[wetland]]s and a biography of Marie-Victorin.<ref name=francoeur/><ref name=sauve/> A great admirer of the man, he had retraced Marie-Victorin's expeditions in Cuba and organized an exposition on the topic.<ref name=sauve/> A founding member of the [[local history]] society of Saint-Anicet, he wrote several accounts of prominent locals such as [[Jules Léger|Jules]] and [[Paul-Émile Léger]], whose families had local ties.<ref name="SHSA"/> He had also been heavily involved on two book projects on the local church and the municipality itself.<ref name="soleil"/>

Bouchard died from a [[heart attack]] on March 4, 2010, in Montreal's [[Central Station (Montreal)|Central Station]], a few months from his planned retirement.<ref name=francoeur/> Bourque presented his condolences,<ref name="condoleances"/>  and flags at the Botanical Garden were flown [[half-staff]] for several days.<ref name="berne"/> He was married with three children.<ref name="fine"/><ref name="pleurent"/> In June of that year, he was a granted a posthumous ''[[honoris causa]]'' doctorate from [[Université Laval]].<ref name="laval"/>
